quick_english: The form-worship should be performed at initiation, consecration, purification of observances, and for the sake of a desired aim; it is of five kinds.
The five types are the single, the paired, the mixed, the circle-joined, and the hero-mingled. The single is done by teachers alone, and the mixed is done by teachers together with others.

The paired worship is done with practitioners and others together with their wives; it is of two kinds, either through union with one's wife or through union with a courtesan who has been brought by payment.
The circle-women and other fitting partners in power-union will be explained later; worship joined with them becomes the circle-joined rite, which grants all fruits.

Then the wise one should first worship the circle in a vessel filled with liquid, placed on a support; satiation should never be done without a support.
Without a support there is a lapse, the radiant powers are not pleased, and the vessel becomes like a ghost, even if it holds śākta nectar and liquor.
There the power is the enjoyer, and that same reality is Śambhu, the supreme lord; thus one should meditate on the united triad of the individual, power, and Śiva.

tokens.grounds: in a rite done for a specific wish
should be performed in the same manner

quick_english: This is the mūrti-yāga, the foremost of all worships; but in a rite performed for a specific desire, it should be done seven times in the same way.
First the Mothers recognize the house, then they perceive its capability and its strength or weakness, and afterward the Mothers are filled with amazement.
Then they draw near, are pleased, and grant boons; and the goddesses and the Lord, together with their retinues, are fully present.

tokens.grounds: female powers together with one another

quick_english: Therefore this beloved mūrti-yāga should be performed by the wise in a pleasing, hidden house, with the heroes and the śaktis fully joined together.
Participants may be brought in without prior arrangement through the recitation of deity names; but if the mūrti circle cannot be obtained, one should worship only maidens.

tokens.grounds: on the first lunar day and under Śravaṇa
and under the three Uttara stars

quick_english: For a desire-rite, one must not choose a maiden who is bodily impaired or menstruating; the rite is also tied to the first lunar day with Śravaṇa and the fourth day with the three Uttara stars.
The fifth day is with Hasta; the sixth with the Pūrva stars and Punarvasu; the seventh and the next with Maghā; and likewise the ninth with Rohiṇī.

tokens.grounds: under Rohiṇī or a Brahma-linked star
on the fourteenth day under Aśvinī

quick_english: The twelfth day is with Mūla, the fourteenth with Aśvinī, the full moon is included, and the new moon is with Dhaniṣṭhā; this forms an elevenfold set.

tokens.grounds: a day joined with Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, or Friday, or another such day

quick_english: A day joined with Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, or Friday, or another suitable day, is well known as a yoga-parvan, whether it occurs by night or by day.
The mūrti-yāga should certainly be performed on a yoga-parvan; the wise person should honor all days called yoga-parvans with the mūrti-yāga.

tokens.grounds: an initiate bound by the vow

quick_english: Through the mūrti-yāga, even without the mandala rite, a person can become a vow-holder; thus is the mūrti-yāga taught in the revered Siddhayogīśvarīmata.

tokens.grounds: in the Ratnamālā and Triśiras texts

quick_english: Now the clear pavitraka rite taught by Śiva is explained, as it has been indicated in the revered Ratnamālā and Triśiras scriptures.

tokens.grounds: in the Siddha, Āṭana, Sadbhāva, Mālinī, and Sāra teachings

quick_english: Among the teachings of the Siddha, Āṭana, Sadbhāva, Mālinī, and Sāra traditions, the procedure taught principally in the revered Mālā is now explained.

tokens.grounds: stupefied by poison-born sleep from the churning of the milk ocean

quick_english: The serpent king, stupefied by a poison-born sleep from the churning of the milk ocean, could not remain in his own realm during the rainy season.
Pure and living only on air, he worshipped Lord Bhairava thoroughly for a hundred divine years, a span multiplied tenfold.
He appealed to the pleased Lord, saying that during the rains he was unable to remain in his own netherworld; and the Supreme Lord responded to him.

tokens.grounds: set upon the seat of his own matted locks
he was supported by all the hosts of gods

quick_english: The Supreme Lord placed the serpent king upon the seat of his own matted locks; then all the hosts of gods bore him upon their heads.

tokens.grounds: therefore on the head of the Great Lord

quick_english: For the great and honored, universal reverence is no wonder; therefore the serpent king came to rest on the head of the Great Lord and, in every way, on the gods as well.

quick_english: Siddhi bearer, mantra power, etc., described elsewhere; those in principle knowledge, mantra, practice, etc.
When those knowers die, they attain union with that Rudra. Yet even after reaching that union, the form it takes varies according to their own latent impressions.
In this way, descents that come from a portion of that Rudra can be highly varied. This is widely reported in the Siddhanta scriptures, in the Puranas, and elsewhere.
Even when all are equally descents of Rudra, their actions and experiences differ. This is because the form of any being is made up of many different powers.
A being is not something apart from its powers; it exists only as their collection. Therefore, what descends as a portion from Rudra and the rest is a particular configuration of powers.

A portion descends so that the task suited to it can clearly be accomplished. The verse then turns to those who, after receiving initiation at a lower level, abandon their faith in it for something higher.
Those who die fixed in that lower level still attain its highest reach. But those who let go of that elevation attain what lies above it.
Even those initiated into a higher level, if they lack sufficient discernment, may reach only a lower end of it. Still, they partake of the fruit of that initiation.
Such people do not abandon their faith in that initiation, even if it rests on scriptural authority. Lacking discernment, they hold to it on the strength of scripture and common repute.
The Supreme Lord taught that one who is merely a bound soul attains the same world, the initiated attains nearness, and one who is devoted to that path attains union.
If someone who follows the higher teaching abandons faith in it through doubt, then even when going to its abode he obtains no fruit at all.
On this point the God of gods said that for such a person initiation, knowledge, and even sacred places are in vain, and so on, as explained in detail elsewhere.
Even if someone is unfit at first, if he remains steadfast in the abode of Shiva, then through that enduring bond of faith he will later obtain that very fruit.
Merit gained from places like rivers, mountains, and pools is not the highest thing at death. Those who die with that merit enjoy the pleasures of heaven.
Those who had gained knowledge and discernment, but near death take refuge in lower abodes, become veiled there.

This is described as a defilement of their knowledge and may indeed count as sin. The established view is that it is removed through the proper sequence of initiation into the lords of those respective realms.
But those who, in mind and conduct, defile initiation, sacred abodes, and knowledge all go to hell.
The loss of one's bond of faith in knowledge, sacred abodes, and initiation is to be recognized by disturbed activities, and those activities are of two kinds.
Some disturbances never arise when a person is healthy and appear only in illness, caused by bodily imbalance. These amount only to the experience of that condition.
Bodily imbalance may awaken old worldly impressions, and they may slip in through temporary openings. But if they have mostly been burned by knowledge, they cannot grow again.
But in those oriented toward isolation, some impressions never appear in good health and yet open up in illness. These arise from the descent of power.
Ordinary worldly impressions are formed by long, deep habituation from the past. As the Lord of Serpents said in the sutra, they appear in those openings.

In those oriented toward isolation, some cognitions arise that were never practiced before. Because of the nature of transmigration, these cannot come from habit and must come from the descent of power.
These disturbed activities, when aggravated by bodily imbalance, lack settled certainty and reflective awareness, and they resemble the behavior of someone asleep or intoxicated.
Even if disturbed behavior seems perverse and appears to defile knowledge, initiation, or the teacher, it should not be taken as true veiling when it has not taken root in the heart.

quick_english: For this very reason, even an awakened person, while still in the body, may undergo karma-born experiences at death, such as visions of Yama's servants, snakes, and the like.
This alone does not mean he is not liberated, for death is an experience just like birth and ongoing life. Therefore death can be of two kinds, involving pain or pleasure.
So, just as the varied pleasures and pains of life do not destroy the liberated state of an awakened person, those same kinds of experiences at death do not destroy it either.
But those yogins who have become well established in a particular principle fix their mind on that very principle and, without doubt, go to it.

This is stated in the revered Svacchanda Tantra, beginning with the teaching about those who die through concentration on fragrance, and likewise the Malini scripture gives the fruits of the various concentrations.
For those who quickly abandon the body through concentrations, as if entering another body, there is no experience that can properly be called death.
The ordinary experience of death consists in a cutting shock at the vital points, delusion spreading through the senses, and a mental sinking into darkness. None of this is found in these yogins.
For the yogin maintains mental effort, establishing an I-sense in another body, as long as the movement of intellect continues there.
The circle of breath, dependent on that same process, moves along the path, and by that very means the circle of senses in the other body becomes awakened.
Just as bees rise when the bee-king rises and settle when he settles, so all the activities of the senses follow the mind.
Therefore, when he moves into another body, there is no inward merging of the senses as in ordinary death. Instead, a subtle continuity arises again, like a body.
Thus, for yogins who move into other bodies and likewise for those who move within bodies formed of various principles, there is no delusion.
These yogins should be known as twofold: worldly and initiated. The former become Shiva gradually, while the latter do so merely through experiencing that state.

quick_english: The teacher should give an explanation of such a scripture to his own student, or even to another's student, if the person is fit to hear it—even to a Vaiṣṇava or someone of a lower affiliation.
A teacher filled with compassion may explain even to a low person, while avoiding the vital secret matters, because the descent of power can occur in many different ways.
On a smeared, square seat on the ground, one should make three lotuses. On the lotus, one should make the seat of knowledge, measuring six and three finger-widths.
In the middle one should worship Vāgīśānī; on the south and north, the teachers and Gaṇeśa; and on the lower lotus, the lord of the ritual tradition, using offering water, flowers, and libations.
Using the offering vessel as in the general rite, the wise teacher should properly satisfy the circle and then give the explanation, beginning with the proper connection.
By connecting aphorism, word, sentence, chapter, and the whole text in order, and by supporting an unbroken link between what comes before and after, one should lead the sentences forward.

Using principles such as the frog-leap and the lion-glance as appropriate, one should present the meaning of the scripture clearly, without mixing it up and without breaking the link between what comes before and after.

One who understands sentences should explain the subject using sound reasoning—such as repetition, contradiction, unwanted consequence, and inference—while keeping it clearly distinct from other matters.
Whatever point comes up in the explanation should be supported with very firm reasoning, even if it is something that will later be refuted.
When the subject is taught by first setting out a firmly formed prior view and then resolving it, it quickly enters the student's mind, free from doubt and misunderstanding.
Whatever language, reasoning, style of discussion, level of absorption, or order becomes a means of awakening for the student, the teacher should adopt that form of explanation.
After completing the subject being explained, there should be satisfaction and worship in the circle. Another subject may be taught after a chapter, but there should be no idle talk.

At the end of the explanation, one should ask forgiveness, dismiss everything, and cast the remains into deep water. Worship should be performed especially at the beginning, middle, and end of the scripture.
At the completion, one should perform special worship for the initiates. Even so, for one whose mind is undivided, there may be no need for expiations.

Even so, for the grace of those who do not know the truth, one should act as taught in the revered Picu scripture. But if remembrance alone destroys sin, O Lord, how can an expiation rite still be prescribed?
When the Goddess asked why an expiation rite is declared, the answer is: it is true that remembrance alone, even uttered once, can liberate one here.
For one who knows remembrance and its truth, liberation from the whole net of action is possible; nevertheless, the rite is enjoined as something to be done for the protection of order.
Those who do not know the truth and are devoted only to ritual conduct suffer a loss of knowledge when their minds begin to waver.
Therefore, if one is free from doubt, one should remain discreet and avoid causing confusion when among those who depend on scripture and ritual conduct.
If confusion of practice arises, one should seek and perform expiation, so that the minds of others do not become unsteady about the meaning of scripture.
In the rite called Shiva-hand it was formerly enjoined that, by reciting this weapon mantra a hundred times, one is freed, except in the case of killing a woman.
The revered Ratnamala says, O beloved, that when a vow is transgressed, the destruction of a woman is a great fault leading to everlasting hell.
For those born in the Kula, an expiation called the wicked knife has been declared; and in the revered earlier text, a purification of the vows is enjoined as follows.
If an installed sacred object and the like is seen by someone without authority, Malini or Matrika should be recited, up to three hundred thousand times.
In the revered Brahmayamala it is said that expiation must be performed by a killer of a brahmin, by one who violates the guru's bed, and likewise by one who steals the hero-substance.
Also included are one who takes the property of the gods or strikes a sacred form, one who breaks the linga, and one who neglects the daily rites and has fallen from his proper measure and equipment.
One who maims Shakti or kills a yogin or knower, or who disrupts the occasional rites, should recite in a doubling sequence beginning with a hundred thousand.
If someone under a vow, eating moderately and observing celibacy, goes elsewhere to take a messenger woman, deluded by desire, that is an offense.
Then one should perform a recitation of a hundred thousand, as stated in the Brahmayamala; and at the end of initiation, consecration, and occasional rites, worship of the guru is required.

According to the teaching of the Siddhayogishvari, it should always be done on the next day: worship of a guru endowed with the previously stated marks, a seer who knows the true principle of the Trika.
That guru should always be accepted, leaving aside any other, even one present in the circle. One should make a svastika there and place upon it a golden or similar seat.
Having prepared the seat, one should worship the path present there in its full extent; then, with devotion, one should request the guru to preside there.
There he should be worshiped with his own mantras, in due order, with flowers, incense, arghya, respectful touching, fine garments, food offerings, and libations.
After worshiping him fully, even to the directions, the disciple should honor him with gifts, offering all he has and, with devout awareness, even himself.
By fully satisfying the guru with gifts, even one who knows the truth is freed from the bond of debt and thereby attains proper fitness for authority.
According to the Skandayamala, one who does not perform guru worship is born for a hundred lifetimes and only then becomes fit for authority and attains liberation.
Therefore a gift must certainly be given again to the guru: earlier it was declared as part of the rite, but this giving is for his satisfaction.
Then, having received his permission, the disciple may partake of what the guru has accepted; after that, he should worship the circle according to the resources available.
Without performing the teacher sacrifice, even completed rites remain undone; therefore the teacher sacrifice must be performed diligently according to one's strength.
Even if the teacher stays there, he is worshipful; having resolved as before, that substance should be used in the deity rite for devotees.
This rite is occasional, distinguished by parva, pavitra, and the rest.
